without, and runs about −0.05 against −0.08; in 2024 the two were nearly identical, and in 2022
passes *without* motion did better.[^epa] Teams that motion more did have slightly better
offenses in each of the four seasons, but the relationship is loose.

::: {.callout-caution title="Common misconception"}
"Motion plays gain more, so offenses should motion on every play." The averages above don't show
that, and even if they did, the comparison wouldn't prove it. Offenses *choose* when to motion:
some save it for their best-designed plays, some motion on almost everything, and defenses adjust
to teams that motion a lot. The plays with and without motion aren't a controlled experiment.
Analysts who try to correct for the situation and the play type tend to find a modest benefit;
ESPN's work, as reported by The Ringer in 2024, put motion at the snap at roughly +0.11 EPA per
play on runs and +0.08 on passes.[^ringer2] <!-- VERIFY: the +0.11 / +0.08 EPA estimates and how ESPN derived them (model-adjusted or raw). -->
Part of motion's value is also invisible in its own plays: a motion that always meant "run" would
be a [tell](../01-foundations/01-06-how-to-watch-a-broadcast.qmd), so offenses use the same
motions on different plays to keep the defense from reading them. Measuring that kind of value is
part of [Tendencies: PROE, Personnel, Motion, and Coverage](../13-analytics-and-data/13-04-tendencies-proe-and-charting.qmd).
:::

## Film room

::: {.callout-note title="Film room: Miami Dolphins 2023, motion at the snap"}
No offense in the tracking era moved like Mike McDaniel's 2023 Dolphins. In FTN's charting they
used motion on 79.4% of their runs and passes, the highest team-season from 2022 to 2025; ESPN had
them with a player in motion at the snap on 59% of plays early that season, a record. They
scored 70 points against Denver in Week 3, and Tyreek Hill led the NFL with 1,799 receiving
yards.[^hill] <!-- VERIFY: Hill 2023 receiving yards (1,799) and Dolphins 70-20 vs Denver, Week 3 2023, on PFR. -->

What to notice when you watch the film: the motion is short and *timed*. Hill or Jaylen Waddle
glides or jogs a few yards, often toward the formation, and the ball is snapped as he gets going.
The defense rarely gets a clean look at its own assignment, and Hill starts every route already
running. Watch the cornerbacks: against Miami, many played off the line, because pressing a
receiver who is in motion is almost impossible. And notice the cost the league imposed: the 2024
language on stops after a backward step from the line was written with this offense in
mind. McDaniel was let go by Miami in January 2026 and is the Chargers' offensive
coordinator for the 2026 season.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Film room: Kansas City Chiefs, Super Bowl LVII (February 12, 2023)"}
Two of the most famous motion plays of the decade came eight minutes apart. In the fourth quarter
against the Eagles, Kansas City ran a play its coaches call "Corn Dog": a receiver motions in
toward the formation, then turns and runs back toward the sideline at the snap, a return motion
built to beat man coverage. Kadarius Toney caught a 5-yard touchdown on it with 12:04 left to give
the Chiefs the lead, and Skyy Moore scored from 4 yards on a mirrored version at 9:22. Both times
the Eagles were in man coverage, the defender went with the first move, and the receiver was alone
when he turned around. Kansas City won 38–35. A year later in Super Bowl LVIII the Chiefs ran a
renamed relative of the play for Mecole Hardman's winning touchdown in overtime.[^corndog] <!-- VERIFY: that the LVIII walk-off was a variant of Corn Dog ('Tom and Jerry'), as reported. -->

What to notice: the motion does *two* jobs on one play. First it asks the question (did the
defender follow?), and then it attacks the answer (the defender who followed is moving the wrong
way). Andy Reid's offense has used motion that way for years, including orbit motion that loops a
receiver behind the quarterback to set up pitches, screens and shovel passes back the other way.
<!-- VERIFY: characterisation of the Chiefs' habitual use of orbit motion (examples and seasons). -->
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Film room: San Francisco 49ers 2021, Deebo Samuel"}
In 2021 the 49ers motioned on 76.9% of their plays, the most in the league by ESPN's count.
Much of it went through Deebo Samuel, a wide receiver who spent part of the season lining up and
motioning into the backfield. Motion let Shanahan move Samuel from receiver to ball carrier and
back again before the snap, so the defense never knew which position it was defending. He caught
passes for 1,405 yards and ran for 365 more, with eight rushing touchdowns.[^deebo] <!-- VERIFY: Samuel 2021 totals on PFR. -->

What to notice: the motion *creates the matchup*. When Samuel motioned from a receiver spot into the
backfield, the defender assigned to him in man coverage had to follow him into the box, where a
cornerback or safety is suddenly playing run defense against a 215-pound receiver with a head start.
Against zone, the defense now faced a backfield with two ball carriers in it, one of them very fast,
and had to respect both.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Film room: Los Angeles Rams 2017–2025, the same look, different plays"}
McVay's Rams were not the league's most frequent motion team in his first seasons (ESPN had them
eighth from 2017 to 2021), but they made the jet motion famous, and by 2024 FTN charted
them with motion on 76.7% of their plays, the highest in the league that season. The Rams' trademark
is pairing: a jet motion that comes before an outside zone run one play, a jet sweep the next and a
play-action pass the play after that, all from the same look, so the motion tells the defense
nothing about the play. What to notice: watch the linebackers when the jet man crosses the
quarterback. If they jump toward him, the next jet is likely to be a fake with the run going the
other way; if they stay home, the jet man himself gets the ball.
:::

## The checklist so far

Part 2 ends here, and with it the first version of the card you will carry through the rest of
the book. Each line is a question you can answer before the snap, in the order the answers
become visible on a broadcast (the order [Personnel](02-01-personnel-groupings.qmd) introduced):
the situation first, then who is on the field, then where they line up, then what the motion
draws out of the defense, then the box and the safeties.

```{python}
#| label: fig-checklist
#| fig-cap: "The watching checklist after Part 2. Line 1 comes from Part 1; lines 2 to 6 are the pre-snap reads Part 2 taught, in the order they become visible during a snap; line 7 is the habit from How to Watch a Broadcast. The motion line is this chapter's. The card grows after Parts 4, 6 and 7, and becomes the master checklist of the capstone."
items = [
    ("BEFORE THE SNAP", None, None, False),
    ("1", "Situation: down, distance, field zone, clock and score", "Part 1", False),
    ("2", "Personnel: who is on the field for each side (two digits for the offense; base, nickel or dime)",
     "02-01, 02-05", True),
    ("3", "Formation and strength: under center or gun, 2x2 or 3x1, where is the tight end?", "02-02 to 02-04", True),
    ("4", "Motion: does a defender travel (man), do they bump (zone), does a safety spin (one-high)? "
          "Is the ball snapped while he's still moving?", "02-06", True),
    ("5", "Box count: blockers against defenders near the line (light box: run; loaded box: pass)", "02-05", True),
    ("6", "Shell: one-high or two-high? Did the motion change it?", "02-05, 02-06", True),
    ("AFTER THE PLAY", None, None, False),
    ("7", "Log it: your run/pass and man/zone calls against what happened", "01-06, 02-06", False),
]
rows = []
for num, text, where, new in items:
    if text is None:
        rows.append(("head", num, 1))
    else:
        lines_ = textwrap.wrap(text, 62)
        rows.append(("item", (num, lines_, where, new), len(lines_)))
n_lines = sum(h for _, _, h in rows) + 4
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.5, 0.24 * n_lines))
ax.set_xlim(0, 100); ax.set_ylim(0, n_lines); ax.axis("off")
ax.add_patch(FancyBboxPatch((0.8, 0.3), 98.4, n_lines - 0.6, boxstyle="round,pad=0.2,rounding_size=0.8",
                            fc=style.SURFACE, ec=style.BASELINE, lw=1.2))
ax.text(3, n_lines - 1.3, "Watching checklist · after Part 2", fontsize=11, fontweight="bold", color=style.INK,
        va="center")
ax.text(97, n_lines - 1.3, "new in Part 2", fontsize=8, color=style.INK_2, ha="right", va="center",
        bbox=dict(boxstyle="round,pad=0.3", fc=style.OFFENSE_TINT, ec="none"))
yy = n_lines - 2.8
for kind, payload, h in rows:
    if kind == "head":
        ax.text(3, yy, payload, fontsize=8, fontweight="bold", color=style.INK_2, va="center")
        yy -= 1.0
        continue
    num, lines_, where, new = payload
    top, bottom = yy + 0.45, yy - (h - 1) - 0.45
    if new:
        ax.add_patch(FancyBboxPatch((2.2, bottom), 95.6, top - bottom, boxstyle="round,pad=0.05,rounding_size=0.4",
                                    fc=style.OFFENSE_TINT, ec="none"))
    ax.text(5.5, yy, num, fontsize=8.5, fontweight="bold", color=style.OFFENSE_DARK, va="center", ha="center")
    for j, ln in enumerate(lines_):
        ax.text(9.0, yy - j, ln, fontsize=8, color=style.INK, va="center")
    ax.text(97, yy, where, fontsize=7, color=style.INK_2, va="center", ha="right")
    yy -= h + 0.15
plt.show()
```

Two habits make the card work. **Say each answer out loud, or write it down, before the snap.**
A guess you didn't commit to can't teach you anything. And **read the lines in order.** The motion
line comes after the formation line because you can't interpret a defender's reaction until you
know what the motion did to the formation; the shell line comes last because the motion may have
changed it.

## Watch for it on Sunday

::: {.callout-tip title="Watch for it: follow the motion"}
For one quarter, every time an offensive player moves before the snap, do four things.

- **Name it.** Jet, orbit, return, zoom, glide, short, a trade, a shift? If you aren't sure, describe
  the path ("across, in front of the quarterback").
- **Watch who follows.** Pick up the defender who was across from the motion man *before* he moved.
  Did that defender travel across (T), did the defenders bump over (B), did a safety spin (S)? Write
  the letters.
- **Call it.** Man or zone? One-high or two-high at the snap? Write your call before the ball is
  snapped.
- **Note the timing.** Was the ball snapped while he was still moving (motion at the snap), or did he
  set first?

Then check your calls on the replay, or better, on the All-22 film, which shows the whole secondary.
Add a column for it in your prediction log from
[How to Watch a Broadcast](../01-foundations/01-06-how-to-watch-a-broadcast.qmd). After a few games
you'll notice two things: travelers are rarer than you expect (many man defenses exchange instead), and
your calls get better when the motion is at the snap.
:::

## Predict the play

::: {.callout-tip title="Predict the play 1: who went with him?"}
```{python}
#| label: fig-predict-travel
#| fig-cap: "Second-and-7. Before the motion the defense shows two deep safeties. Then H, in the left slot, motions across the formation, and the nickel back (NB, ringed) runs with him the whole way. As he does, the safety on the right (SS) comes down to about 8 yards in the middle of the field and the safety on the left (FS) slides over to the deep middle. Dashed paths are pre-snap movement. The ball is snapped as H reaches the right side."
off = gun_2x2_spread()
dfn = front4(sde=5.0) + [
    D("LCB", "CB", 6.5, -15.5, "CB"), D("RCB", "CB", 6.5, 15.5, "CB"), D("NB", "NB", 5.5, -9.5, "NB"),
    D("MIKE", "MIKE", 4.5, 1.5, "M"), D("WILL", "WILL", 4.5, -2.5, "W"), D("SS", "SS", 13.0, 8.5, "SS"),
    D("FS", "FS", 13.0, -8.5, "FS")]
q = Play(off, dfn, los=45, to_go=7)
q.motion("H", pts=[(-1.0, 5.0), (-1.3, 14.0), (-0.5, 20.0), (-0.5, 21.0)])
q.motion("NB", pts=[(0.5, 4.0), (0.6, 12.0), (0.4, 20.0), (0.3, 21.5)])
dashed_motion(q, "SS", (9.2, -0.5))
dashed_motion(q, "FS", (14.0, -0.5))
q.highlight("NB", color=style.THIRD)
fld = q.draw(lateral=(-20.5, 20.5), window=(-7.5, 17.5), title=False)
no_numbers(fld.ax)
P = P_of(fld, q)
tag(fld.ax, P(-5.4, 13.0), "snap as H\narrives", ec=style.THIRD, lw=1.0, fs=7.2)
plt.show()
```

**Man or zone? How many deep safeties? And what does the offense like about the picture?**

::: {.callout-tip title="Answer" collapse="true"}
**Man coverage, with one deep safety: Cover 1, almost certainly.** Two things happened at once.
The nickel back travelled with H all the way across the formation, which a zone defender has no
reason to do: that says man. And the safeties spun: the two-high picture turned into one safety in
the deep middle and one at 8 yards in the middle of the field, a classic spot for a "robber" who
lurks underneath looking for crossing routes (see
[Man Coverage](../06-pass-coverage/06-02-man-coverage.qmd)). Travel plus spin is the signature of
man coverage disguised as two-high before the motion.

What the offense likes: H's defender is now **behind and inside** a receiver who is moving toward
the sideline at full speed. A flat route, a wheel up the sideline, or a quick throw to H the instant
the ball is snapped all start as races the nickel back is losing. On the other side, X is alone
with his corner, and with the single deep safety in the middle there is no help over the top on the
outside. Man coverage also means most defenders have their backs turned to the quarterback, so a
quarterback who can run has open grass if the routes clear out the middle.

The caution: a robber in the middle is there precisely to jump the crossing routes that beat man
coverage, so throwing a shallow cross into him is the mistake the defense is hoping for.
:::
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Predict the play 2: the jet they stopped respecting"}
```{python}
#| label: fig-predict-jet
#| fig-cap: "Third quarter, first-and-10. Six times in the first half the offense ran this exact jet motion by Z and handed the ball to the running back going the other way. This time, as Z sprints across, the linebackers (ringed) don't move with him and the defensive end on the side Z is heading to (E, ringed) squeezes inside toward the running back. The safeties stay where they were. Z is 2 yards from the quarterback when the ball is snapped."
off = gun_2x1_te()
dfn = front4() + [
    D("LCB", "CB", 7.0, -15.5, "CB"), D("RCB", "CB", 7.0, 15.5, "CB"), D("NB", "NB", 5.5, -10.0, "NB"),
    D("MIKE", "MIKE", 4.5, 1.2, "M"), D("WILL", "WILL", 4.5, -2.5, "W"),
    D("FS", "FS", 13.0, -9.0, "FS"), D("SS", "SS", 13.0, 9.0, "SS")]
q = Play(off, dfn, los=40, to_go=10)
q.motion("Z", pts=[(-0.9, -5.0), (-1.4, -10.0), (-1.5, -12.6)])
dashed_motion(q, "WDE", (1.0, -3.4))
q.highlight("MIKE", "WILL", "WDE", color=style.THIRD)
fld = q.draw(lateral=(-20.5, 20.5), window=(-7.5, 15.5), title=False)
no_numbers(fld.ax)
P = P_of(fld, q)
callout(fld.ax, P, "linebackers\nstay home", (9.5, -6.5), (5.0, -1.6), ec=style.THIRD)
callout(fld.ax, P, "end squeezes\ninside", (-4.5, -11.0), (0.7, -3.9), ec=style.THIRD)
plt.show()
```

**What should the offense call here, and why does it work only because of the first half?**

::: {.callout-tip title="Answer" collapse="true"}
**Give the ball to Z: the jet sweep itself.** The defense has learned that the jet is a fake and
the run is coming the other way, so it has stopped spending players on the jet. The linebackers
stay home to play the running back, and the end on Z's side is squeezing inside toward the back's
path. That leaves the edge on the jet side with nobody setting it except a corner who is seven
yards off and blocked by X. Z already has a head start; with the end crashing inside and nobody
flowing with him, he gets the corner.

That is the logic of jet motion as a *constraint*: the fake is only worth something if the real
thing is a threat. Run the inside handoff enough and the defense ignores the jet; run the jet when
it does. Offenses build their game plans around exactly this pairing (more in
[Perimeter Runs and Misdirection](../03-the-run-game/03-05-perimeter-and-misdirection.qmd) and
[Constraint Theory and Sequencing](../08-the-chess-match/08-02-constraint-theory-and-sequencing.qmd)).
The defense's counter is to keep at least one player honest on the jet side: a safety who spins
toward the motion, as in the zone animation earlier, would have been waiting.
:::
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Predict the play 3: the back motions out"}
```{python}
#| label: fig-predict-empty
#| fig-cap: "Third-and-6. The running back (R) motions out of the backfield to the right, leaving an empty backfield. The Mike linebacker (M, ringed) walks out of the box with him and stops across from him near the numbers. Everyone else stays put: one deep safety in the middle, the other safety down at 7 yards over the tight end."
off = gun_2x2_spread()
dfn = front4(sde=5.0) + [
    D("LCB", "CB", 6.0, -15.5, "CB"), D("RCB", "CB", 6.0, 15.5, "CB"), D("NB", "NB", 5.0, -9.5, "NB"),
    D("SS", "SS", 7.5, 8.0, "SS"), D("MIKE", "MIKE", 4.5, 0.8, "M"), D("WILL", "WILL", 4.5, -3.0, "W"),
    D("FS", "FS", 13.5, 0.0, "FS")]
q = Play(off, dfn, los=45, to_go=6)
q.motion("RB", pts=[(1.0, 4.0), (1.8, 10.0), (2.8, 13.0), (3.0, 13.9)])
dashed_motion(q, "MIKE", (4.8, 12.2))
q.highlight("MIKE", color=style.THIRD)
fld = q.draw(lateral=(-20.5, 20.5), window=(-7.5, 16.5), title=False)
no_numbers(fld.ax)
P = P_of(fld, q)
callout(fld.ax, P, "box: 5 defenders", (10.0, -7.0), (4.6, -3.0))
plt.show()
```

**Man or zone? And what has the defense just done to its middle?**

::: {.callout-tip title="Answer" collapse="true"}
**Man coverage.** A middle linebacker has no zone responsibility out near the numbers; the only
reason for him to walk out with the running back is that the back is *his man*. In zone, the
nickel or the safety already standing on that side would simply have taken the back, and the
Mike would have stayed in the box.

What it did to the middle: the box now has five defenders (four linemen and the Will), and the
middle of the field underneath the deep safety has one fewer player in it. With five receivers
out and five blockers, it's also the moment to check the pass protection, because an empty
formation leaves the quarterback with no back to pick up an extra rusher; if a sixth defender
comes, someone has to be thrown to quickly (see
[Pass Protection](../04-the-passing-game/04-02-pass-protection.qmd)). For the play, man coverage
with a linebacker on a running back is a mismatch the offense created on purpose: a quick out or a
wheel route by the back, against a linebacker who has to cover him in space, is often the first
read. And with every defender's back turned, a quarterback scramble up the middle is open on third-and-6.
:::
:::

## Takeaways

- **Motion is never decoration.** Every motion does at least one of five jobs: it asks *man or
  zone?*, changes the strength and the numbers, creates leverage, gives a running start, or stresses
  the defense's communication. Every one costs play-clock time and precise timing, and any motion
  that always means the same play becomes a tell.
- **Learn the shapes, not just the names.** Jet, fly and orbit cross the formation (in front of,
  behind, and looping behind the quarterback); rocket sprints a back to the edge; return goes and
  comes back; zoom crosses and sets; glide and short motion come in; a trade or a shift to bunch
  rebuilds the formation. Names vary by playbook.
- **Read the answer:** a defender who **travels** suggests man; defenders who **bump** suggest zone;
  safeties who **spin** turn two-high into one-high. That's the **man/zone indicator**, and it is a
  hint, not a guarantee: man defenses can exchange, pattern-matching zones can follow, and safeties
  can spin back.
- **The later the motion, the more it's worth.** Motion at the snap gives a running start worth
  about three yards in the first second, and leaves the defense no time to disguise. NFL use of it
  rose from about 4% of plays in 2017 to over 20% by 2023 (ESPN), and the league tightened the rules
  on rolling starts from the line in 2024. American rules allow one man moving sideways or back;
  Canadian rules allow forward motion.
- **Motion numbers depend on the source.** PFF (any shift or motion: 63.9% in 2025), FTN (motion
  before or at the snap: 55.1%), ESPN and Next Gen Stats (motion at the snap) all measure different
  things. Quote one source at a time.
- **The checklist so far:** situation → personnel → formation and strength → the motion response →
  box → shell, then log it.

::: {.callout-note title="Go deeper"}
- **Big Data Bowl 2025** was built around exactly this chapter's question: what pre-snap movement
  reveals about the play. Its files include, for every player on every play from the first nine
  weeks of 2022, flags for whether he was in motion at the snap and whether he shifted or went in
  motion after the line set. Once you have the files, this is how you'd start:

```{python}
#| eval: false
#| echo: true
#| code-summary: "Show the Python (Big Data Bowl 2025: motion flags and coverage)"
import pandas as pd
from gridiron import bdb, show_animation

pp = pd.read_csv("data/bdb/player_play.csv")      # one row per player per play
plays = pd.read_csv("data/bdb/plays.csv")         # one row per play, with PFF's coverage labels
FLAGS = ["inMotionAtBallSnap", "motionSinceLineset", "shiftSinceLineset"]
KEYS = ["gameId", "playId"]
flags = pp.groupby(KEYS)[FLAGS].max().reset_index()          # True if any player did it
flags = flags.merge(plays[KEYS + ["possessionTeam", "pff_manZone"]], on=KEYS)
print(flags[FLAGS].mean())                                   # share of plays with each
print(pd.crosstab(flags.inMotionAtBallSnap, flags.pff_manZone, normalize="index"))

# animate one play with motion at the snap, drawn like this chapter's diagrams
trk = bdb.load_tracking("data/bdb/tracking_week_1.csv")
g, pl = flags.loc[flags.inMotionAtBallSnap == True, KEYS].iloc[0]
show_animation(bdb.prepare(trk, plays, game_id=g, play_id=pl))
```

- Ben Solak's January 2024 piece in *The Ringer* on how the Chiefs' and Ravens' defenses answered
  motion, and Nick Wagoner and Lindsey Thiry's 2022 ESPN piece on Shanahan's and McVay's motion
  habits (both linked in the notes).
- Chris B. Brown, *The Art of Smart Football* (2015), for the older roots of motion and shifts in
  offensive design.
:::
